extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, agency counsel, and rulemaking practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and procedural guidance for when an agency may invoke the APA 'good cause' exception to issue an interim final rule (IFR), and how courts should review such IFRs and related stay petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency justification in light of record and filed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency was not required to justify its decision in light of the record of all the information before the agency, including the filed comments; comments were meant to provide the agency with information that it could consider before using its expert judgment to decide what rule best served the goals of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts review rules under the arbitrary and capricious standard; although comments inform agencies, the agency uses its expertise to decide the rule. This dynamic affects how much post-hoc justification courts will expect depending on the record available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of basis and purpose; reasoned decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires that agencies include a statement of the basis and purpose for a rule when adopting it and judicial review ensures that a rule is not 'arbitrary, capricious, [or] an abuse of discretion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts read the APA’s statement-of-basis-and-purpose requirement together with judicial review to justify rigorous inquiry into agency factfinding, predictions, and reasoning; agencies must provide a rational connection between facts found and choice made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to 'take a hard look' and provide meaningful participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate courts have imposed obligations including that 'the agency must establish a proper framework for principled decision-making,' 'take a hard look' at the issues before it and ensure that interested parties have 'genuine opportunities to participate in a meaningful way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are judicially articulated procedural expectations that go beyond minimal notice-and-comment: agencies should create an adequate record, consider alternatives, and provide meaningful opportunities for participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual APA allowance for good cause when notice-and-comment is contrary to public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA text states that the section on rulemaking does not apply when the agency can show good cause that notice-and-comment would 'be contrary to the public interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This textual provision supports agency invocation of good cause/IFRs when doing so best serves the public interest, though critics argue this may conflict with Congress's intent; the article treats the statutory text as permitting IFRs in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency commitment to consider comments and finalize via FFR
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuance of an IFR commits the agency to allow and consider comments on the IFR and ultimately to adopt a final final rule (FFR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IFR delays but does not eliminate the notice-and-comment burden; agencies issuing IFRs should commit to subsequent consideration and justification of comments as they would for a NOPR-initiated rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should restrict IFRs to rules with objectively recognized benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility that the lack of notice-and-comment might allow the agency to adopt a rule that is inferior to the status quo ante counsels that courts should restrict the bounds of IFRs to rules with objectively recognized benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To justify invoking good cause, an agency should present credible evidence that the rule will better serve the statutory scheme and the public interest; courts should ask whether the IFR is likely better than the regulatory status quo ante.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency burden of proof: IFR likely objectively better than status quo
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing an IFR, the agency should have the burden of convincing the court that the IFR likely will be objectively better than the regulatory status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must explain how the IFR will affect those intended to be protected, identify evidence supporting the conclusion, need not conduct new studies, must not ignore publicly available information undermining the evaluation, and if evidence is uncertain explain why it is 'more likely than not' the IFR will provide objective benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court deference limits under uncertainty; need for persuasive considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The court should not defer to the agency due to mere uncertainty; an agency must identify the considerations it found persuasive and offer a rational connection between available evidence and the choice made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts often defer on technical matters, agencies must still acknowledge uncertainties and explain why their predictions are reasonable; mere recitation of 'substantial uncertainty' is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Likely superior' preliminary standard for IFR stay decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: For the limited question of whether to stay an IFR because it was issued prior to the opportunity for comment, judges should address simply whether the rule is likely better than the regulatory status quo ante, using a 'likely superior' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is similar to the 'likelihood of success' inquiry in preliminary injunctions: it is a preliminary, less-demanding assessment made before a full record develops, and if the agency can show the IFR is likely superior the court should not stay it solely on procedural grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-limited expedited review of stay petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: One way for courts to assure timely review is to expedite consideration of a petition to stay an IFR solely on grounds that the IFR is not justified under the good cause standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such expedited review would focus only on whether the IFR is justified as good cause for pre-notice-and-comment promulgation, not on the agency's legal authority or the merits under arbitrary-and-capricious review; this limits issues and speeds judicial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should evaluate IFR pathologies when deciding propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential pathologies of an IFR that courts should evaluate include: that the IFR is not better than the regulatory status quo ante; the agency might abuse the IFR to adopt a politically preferred rule that notice-and-comment would prevent; and the IFR will bias subsequent consideration of comments so the FFR serves the public interest less well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of the specific pathology, the ultimate question is whether the benefit of decreased regulatory delay exceeds the costs of adopting a less-than-ideal FFR; courts should assess these harms when deciding to stay or allow an IFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFRs can cause lasting or permanent harms; need for quick judicial check
rubrics_metrics.description: Although IFRs may be temporary, their issuance can cause harm that extends beyond their duration and might be permanent, so it is crucial that courts can quickly review IFR propriety to ensure they do not cause more harm than good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies can issue an FFR before a court fully reviews an IFR challenge, courts should have mechanisms (e.g., expedited stays) to address potential irreversible harms caused during the IFR period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requiring sunset/commitment mechanisms to bind IFRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring an agency to commit to a sunset provision in an IFR will ensure that the agency must defend the ultimate rule that it adopts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposing procedural commitments (such as sunsets or an obligation to finalize/defend an FFR) increases the resource cost to the agency of issuing an IFR and can discourage frivolous or opportunistic use of the good cause exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFR issuance does not alter nature of judicial review for resulting FFR
rubrics_metrics.description: The issuance of an IFR does not alter the nature of judicial review of the resulting FFR; the agency remains subject to arbitrary-and-capricious review when it adopts its final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an agency uses an IFR to act quickly, it remains obligated to consider comments and to justify its final decision under existing standards of reasoned decisionmaking; procedural defects in an IFR may complicate but do not eliminate review of the FFR.
